## What happened

Someone pushed new commits to `main` on `github.com:acme/widgets.git`. Your local `main` does not contain those commits. Your local branch and the remote branch now share a common ancestor only. Git stops the push, because a successful push would drop that remote work. Nothing changed. Your commits are still safe in your local repository.

## What to do

1. Run `git fetch origin`. This downloads the remote commits. It changes no local branch.
2. Run `git log --oneline main..origin/main`. This shows you the commits that you do not have.
3. Put your work on top of the remote work. Run `git rebase origin/main`.
4. Fix any conflict that the rebase reports. Then run `git rebase --continue`.
5. Run `git push` again.

`git pull --rebase` does steps 1 and 3 in one command.

## Rebase or merge

Rebase moves your commits on top of the remote commits. The history stays linear. Your commits get new hashes. Use rebase when your commits are local only.

Merge keeps both histories. It adds one merge commit. Use merge when you already pushed your commits to a shared branch, or when your team prefers merge commits.

## One warning

Do not run `git push --force`. Force push deletes the other person's commits from the remote. `--force-with-lease` is safer, but it is also the wrong tool here. The correct fix is to integrate the remote work first.

One more check: step 2 tells you what the new remote commits are. Read that list before you rebase. An unexpected commit on `main` can mean that someone pushed to the wrong branch.
